Learning Objectives
Understand the epidemiology of intraoperative neurovascular injuries in total hip and knee
arthroplasty.
Understand the relevant anatomy and risk factors associated with neurovascular injury.
Diagnose neurovascular injury in hip and knee arthroplasty.
Implement surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for the management of neurovascular
injury.
Nerve Injury: Total Hip and Knee Arthroplasty
Overview
The constellation of symptoms associated with damage to nerves during total hip and knee
arthroplasty




NOTES

Epidemiology
Relatively uncommon
Approximate prevalence for nerve injury is 0.9% and 2.6% for primary total hip arthroplasty
and revision total hip arthroplasty, respectively, and approximately 0.3% and 2% for primary
total knee arthroplasty and revision knee arthroplasty, respectively.1
For total hip arthroplasty, sciatic nerve injuries are the most common (usually the peroneal
branch), followed by femoral, obturator, and superior gluteal nerve injuries. The lateral
femoral cutaneous nerve is commonly injured after direct anterior hip arthroplasty; however,
it rarely results in functional limitations for patients.
The peroneal nerve is the functional nerve at risk during total knee arthroplasty.
For hip arthroplasty, risk factors include female sex, developmental dysplasia, anatomic
abnormalities or severe contractures, and the need for limb lengthening.
For knee arthroplasty, anatomic risk factors include valgus deformity and flexion contracture.
Metabolic or extra-articular anatomic disorders that make nerves generally more susceptible
to injury include diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, and spinal stenosis.

Epidemiology
Nerve injury is relatively uncommon after total hip or knee arthroplasty but may be
devastating for patients. Depending on the study, the incidence ranges from less than
1% for primary surgery to 3% for revision surgery. The true prevalence may be much
higher because electromyographic (EMG) testing often reveals a higher rate of injury;
however, most of these injuries are subclinical and are not associated with long-term
functional consequences. A number of risk factors exist; however, many are not
modifiable.
Anatomy
The femoral nerve lies on the iliopsoas muscle and courses anterior to the acetabulum.
The sciatic nerve exits the sciatic notch and has a variable course after exiting the pelvis with
respect to the piriformis muscle.

The superior gluteal nerve exits the sciatic foramen and traverses above the piriformis along
the superior portion of the acetabulum.
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve emerges at the lateral edge of the psoas muscle, below
the ilioinguinal nerve, and then passes beneath the iliac fascia and the inguinal ligament.
The peroneal nerve is the lateral division of the sciatic nerve and courses around the lateral
aspect of the knee around the fibular head.

Anatomy
Nerves are at risk during total hip or knee arthroplasty because of their relevant
anatomy and proximity to the joint. Surgeons must understand the course of each nerve
as it relates to surgery. The femoral nerve is closest to the acetabulum at the inferior
border above the pubic ramus (approximately 1 cm) and farthest away at the 12-o’clock
position (approximately 2.5 cm; Figure 1). The sciatic nerve is tethered at the sciatic
notch. In most patients, the tibial and peroneal divisions exit anterior and below the
piriformis; however, variants in which one division exits above or through the piriformis
may be more susceptible to injury. The nerve is approximately 1.75 cm away from the 9-
o’clock position and is closest to the ischial tuberosity. The tibial division contains more
fascicles and connective tissue and, therefore, is less susceptible to compression injuries
(Figure 2). The superior gluteal nerve is farthest away posteriorly and closer anteriorly,
coursing approximately 3 cm from the anterior tip of the greater trochanter (Figure 3).
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve exits medial to the anterior superior iliac spine
(approximately 2 cm) in most patients and medial to the sartorius muscle with highly
variable branching. Specific approaches to the hip are associated with specific nerve
injury risks; however, a risk of injury to all nerves can occur with each approach.
Posterior approaches are associated with the highest risk of sciatic nerve injury; lateral
approaches are associated with a higher risk of superior gluteal nerve injury; and
anterior approaches are associated with a higher risk of femoral and lateral femoral
cutaneous nerve injury. The peroneal nerve is tethered at the fibular head and is closest
to the knee joint at the posterolateral corner of the tibia (approximately 1 cm). A clear
understanding of the anatomy of nerves at risk will inform surgical dissection and
retractor placement.

Etiology
The etiology of intraoperative nerve injury is not fully understood but may result from direct
injury, compression, ischemia, or traction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
5/19

Direct injury may result from lacerations caused by scalpels, retractor tips, saw blades, drills or
screws, bone fragments, or placement of wires and cables.
Compression and ischemia may result from retractors, limb positioning, hematoma formation,
or cement extrusion (which also may cause thermal injury).
Traction may be caused by limb manipulation or positioning, deformity correction, or retractor
placement.
The Seddon classification generally is used to describe the specific anatomic etiology of injury
as it relates to severity and prognosis.

Etiology
The etiology of intraoperative nerve injury is not fully understood, with various possible
mechanisms of injury in each patient.2, 3 The Seddon classification offers an anatomic
basis for the degree of injury that also is useful for predicting recovery.4 Neurapraxia is a
failure of neural conduction resulting from altered nerve physiology in a patient with an
intact neurologic structure and is associated with the best prognosis for recovery.
Patients with axonotmesis have some disruption of axons and distal degeneration of
myelin (Wallerian degeneration) but the endoneurial tube remains intact. Neurotmesis
consists of complete disruption of the nerve and is associated with the poorest
prognosis.
Preoperative Evaluation and Management
Preoperative risk factors should be clearly identified and incorporated in the discussion of
risks and advantages with the patient.
A thorough physical examination should be documented; if any abnormal findings are
identified, additional investigation should be pursued.
Spinal decompression may be warranted before hip or knee arthroplasty to avoid a double-
crush phenomenon.

Preoperative Evaluation and Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
6/19

Preoperative evaluation and management may help decrease the risks of nerve injury.
Identification of risk factors warrants clear discussion with the patient. If any neurologic
concerns exist regarding symptoms and physical examination findings, EMG or a
neurologic consultation may be helpful. Surgeons should consider decompression of the
spine in patients with severe stenosis to decrease the risks of a double-crush injury.
Intraoperative Risk Mitigation
A thorough understanding of patient anatomy and the surgical approach is critical to decrease
the risks of nerve injury.
Surgeons should adhere to careful retractor placement, limit limb immobilization, and avoid
placing nerves on tension.
Femoral shortening osteotomy may be necessary, particularly in patients with dysplasia in
whom limb lengthening is necessary.
Limited neurolysis of the sciatic nerve may be useful in revision procedures.
Appropriate soft-tissue releases and bone resection should be performed during total knee
arthroplasty in patients with valgus or flexion deformities.
Intraoperative neuromonitoring may be used in high-risk patients.

Intraoperative Risk Mitigation
Prevention of nerve injury requires diligence by the surgeon. Placement of retractors
around the acetabulum and the lateral aspect of the knee should be performed carefully
and as safely as possible, using knowledge of specific anatomy to distance retractors
from nerves if possible. The surgeon should be cognizant of avoiding positions that
create traction on nerves based on a specific approach. For example, the surgeon may
want to avoid hip flexion if a posterior retractor is placed during a posterior approach or
avoid hip extension if an anterior retractor is placed for an anterior approach. The
surgeon should be aware of and direct assistants to minimize pressure placed on
retractors if possible. Soft-tissue dissection should be as limited as much as possible in
areas at which nerves are at risk. In a knee with a flexion contracture, the surgeon
should ensure that adequate bone is resected to correct the deformity without forceful
pressure causing traction on the nerve. For hip arthroplasty procedures in which femoral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
7/19

lengthening is expected, femoral shortening osteotomy should be considered.5 This is
particularly true for patients with dysplasia. Preoperative planning is critical for risk
mitigation in situations in which lengthening of more than 4 cm can be predicted. Lateral
releases for the valgus knee should be performed carefully, and cautery used for this
purpose should be limited to avoid risk of thermal injury to the nerve. For high-risk
patients, interoperative neuromonitoring via motor-evoked potentials and
somatosensory-evoked potentials can be used for immediate intraoperative feedback.
Management
In the rare event of a recognized direct injury, repair should be undertaken intraoperatively or
as soon as possible.
A thorough motor and sensory examination should be performed for all patients
postoperatively. For patients with spine or regional anesthesia still in effect, multiple
examinations may be necessary.
If a nerve injury is identified immediately postoperatively, the nerve limb should be positioned
to relax the nerve, and hematoma or external compression should be ruled out. Serial
examinations should be undertaken.
The patient should be thoroughly educated about the nerve injury.
Orthoses and braces should be used to maximize function and minimize contractures.
Consultation with neurology and electrodiagnostic studies may be helpful during recovery
(Resources 1 and 2).

Management
For nerves that are injured directly and the injury is recognized intraoperatively, direct
repair should be undertaken.6 In the immediate postoperative period, a thorough motor
and sensory examination should be undertaken, with serial examinations as indicated,
depending on the presence of spinal or regional anesthesia. In many patients, an
apparent peroneal nerve injury after knee replacement may simply be the result of
periarticular injections tracking along the nerve and may resolve within 24 hours. If a
postoperative examination is concerning for nerve injury, the limb should be examined
for any external compression from bandages or braces and positioned to take tension
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
8/19

off the nerve (hip extension and knee flexion for the sciatic nerve, hip flexion and knee
extension for the femoral nerve, and knee flexion for the peroneal nerve). Hematoma
should be considered, especially with a worsening examination or in patients on
aggressive anticoagulation, and cross-sectional imaging studies should be obtained with
urgent surgical management warranted after a diagnosis is made. Surgical evacuation of
the hematoma and hemostasis should be performed emergently to maximize the
likelihood of recovery and minimize ongoing compressive injury. Other causes of direct
nerve compression also should be ruled out, including obtaining an MRI of the lumbar
spine to evaluate for lumbar disk herniation. If no specific cause of nerve injury is
identified immediately, then expectant management is performed. This includes
extensive patient counseling and avoidance of additional complications. Braces and
orthoses are used to maximize ambulation and minimize contractures. For the sciatic
and peroneal nerves, this includes an ankle-foot orthosis for ankle dorsiflexion. For
femoral nerve injuries, this includes a knee immobilizer or a drop-lock brace. Prolonged
physical therapy is helpful, particularly to keep patients engaged in their recovery.
Neurologic consultation with EMG can be obtained at approximately 6 weeks
postoperatively to aid in prognosis. Fibrillations are a poor prognostic sign, suggesting
the discontinuity of axons and the denervation of muscle. If evidence of neural
regeneration is present, expectant management is continued. The Tinel sign denotes at
least partial nerve continuity, and an advancing Tinel sign also suggests recovery.
Clinically, the Tinel sign may progress until the nerve encounters a secondary site of
compression (the fibular head for the peroneal nerve and the medial/lateral plantar
tunnels for the tibial nerve). If nerve recovery does not progress, then surgical
decompression of these secondary sites is considered. Follow-up EMG should be
performed 3 months postoperatively. If EMG performed 3 months postoperatively does
not reveal a pattern of regeneration, scarring around the nerve may be present, and the
surgeon should consider performing neurolysis at the site at which injury is most likely
to have occurred. Neurolysis has not been shown to have a detrimental effect and
should be performed within the first year postinjury for maximal improvement.
Importantly, even late neurolysis has been demonstrated to improve pain.
Outcomes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
9/19

Recovery of nerve injuries depends on the degree of injury and the distance to the affected
area.
In general, femoral and peroneal nerve injuries are associated with a better prognosis than
sciatic nerve injuries for recovery.
Recovery may be prolonged, and full recovery may take 2 or 3 years.

Outcomes
The more severe the injury and the greater distance to the affected muscle and sensory
nerves, the more guarded the overall prognosis should be. Axons grow distally at a rate
of approximately 1 mm/day in adults, and motor end plates and muscle fascicles can
atrophy before regenerated axons reach them. The Schwann cell basement membrane
undergoes degeneration with time, which may result in the possibility that axon sprouts
will no longer have a tubular guide. Irreversible muscle fibrosis and motor end plate
degeneration typically occur by 24 months postinjury. Regeneration for a sciatic nerve
injury at the hip has the farthest to travel and, therefore, generally is associated with the
least favorable prognosis. Good prognostic indicators include partial injuries and injuries
with some early motor recovery. Patients should be counseled that recovery may be very
slow, initial recovery may not be observed for many months, and full recovery may take
2 to 3 years.4
Vascular Injury: Total Hip and Knee Arthroplasty
Overview
The constellation of symptoms associated with damage to blood vessels during total hip and
knee arthroplasty
Epidemiology
Very uncommon
Approximate prevalence for vascular injury is 0.2% to 0.3% for primary and revision total hip
arthroplasty and approximately 0.2% or less for primary and revision knee arthroplasty.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
10/19

For total hip arthroplasty, injury most commonly occurs to the external iliac or femoral
arteries; for total knee arthroplasty, injury most commonly occurs to the popliteal artery.
Injuries are most commonly thromboembolic events, followed by lacerations,
pseudoaneurysms, and arteriovenous fistulas.
Risk factors include female sex, prior vascular surgery, vascular disease with calcified and
noncompliant vessels, and prior surgery resulting in anatomic risks of surgical dissection in
proximity to vessels.

Epidemiology
Vascular injury is rare after total hip and knee arthroplasty but may be potentially
devastating for patients. Although the incidence of vascular injury is well below 1%, it is
critical to recognize and manage vascular injury emergently.1 Most injuries are occlusive
thromboembolic events, followed by direct injury from laceration. Pseudoaneurysms
and arteriovenous fistulas are less common and often present later in the postoperative
period. Specific risk factors exist; however, most of these are not modifiable. Prior
vascular, hip, or knee surgery all increase the risk of injury. Calcifications observed on
radiographs have been indicated as a risk factor. Surgical anatomic considerations, such
as hip revision procedures with protrusio or knee revision procedures requiring
considerable posterior dissection also are associated with an increased risk of injury. In
patients with severe peripheral vascular disease warranting revascularization,
revascularization should be performed before hip and knee surgery if possible.
Anatomy
The arterial circulation of the hip and leg begins with the external and internal iliac arteries.
The internal iliac artery branches contribute to the arterial circulation of the gluteal region and
the proximal thigh. The superior gluteal artery exits the sciatic notch and traverses the pelvis
with the superior gluteal nerve. The external iliac artery continues as the femoral artery after it
passes the inguinal ligament.
The deep femoral artery supplies deeper structures of the anterior thigh and also is the main
blood supply of the posterior thigh and the anastomosis around the hip joint.

9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
11/19

The continuation of the femoral artery (the superficial femoral artery) transitions to the
popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus. Branches of the femoral and
popliteal arteries contribute to the anastomosis around the knee. The popliteal artery
ultimately gives rise to the three main arteries that supply the leg.
The vessels are most at risk to direct injury at the location at which they are most proximate to
the surgical field or via penetrating instrumentation. Because the vessels travel with major
nerves in many patients, the same principles for injury risk apply.

Anatomy
Vessels are at risk during total hip or knee arthroplasty because of their relevant
anatomy and proximity to the joint or surgical dissection. An understanding of the
course of each vessel as it relates to the procedure is important. The femoral artery is
closest to the acetabulum at the inferior border above the pubic ramus and farthest at
the 12-o’clock position. The superior gluteal artery is farthest posteriorly and closer
anteriorly. The popliteal artery is closest to the knee at the joint line, approximately 1 cm
and slightly lateral in the posterior aspect of the knee. Specific safe zones for acetabular
screw placement have been well described, with the posterosuperior zone being the
safest, and the anterosuperior zone being the most dangerous (Figure 4). A clear
understanding of the anatomy of vessels at risk will inform surgical dissection and
retractor placement.

Etiology
The etiology of intraoperative vascular injury generally results from direct injury or from
occlusion.
Direct injury may result from lacerations caused by scalpels, retractor tips, saw blades, drills or
screws, bone fragments, or placement of wires and cables. Cement extrusion may cause
thermal injury, leading to pseudoaneurysms or fistulas. In additions, vessels may be injured
from adherence to scar tissue during dissection.
Occlusion may result from thromboembolic events. Often, these may not be directly related to
surgical technique but may be precipitated by tourniquet use, retractors, limb positioning,
manipulations, hematoma formation, or cement extrusion.

Etiology
The etiology of intraoperative vascular injury generally is from direct trauma to vessels
or from thromboembolic occlusion. Direct injury may result from a number of
mechanisms, and thromboembolism may be precipitated by various aspects of the
surgical procedure.
Preoperative Evaluation and Management
Preoperative risk factors should be clearly identified and incorporated in the discussion of
risks and advantages with the patient.
A thorough physical examination should be documented; if any abnormal findings are
identified, additional investigation should be pursued.
Evaluation by a vascular surgeon and revascularization may be warranted before hip or knee
surgery.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
14/19


Preoperative Evaluation and Management
Preoperative evaluation and management may help decrease the risks of vascular injury.
Identification of risk factors warrants clear discussion with the patient. Distal pulses
should be clearly palpable or evaluated via Doppler examination. If blood flow is
questionable, then an ankle-brachial index should be calculated. An ankle-brachial index
of less than 0.5 warrants vascular consultation and additional evaluation.
Revascularization for claudication may be warranted before proceeding with hip or knee
surgery. In patients with high-risk anatomy or surgical considerations (such as severe
protrusio), CT angiography may be useful to visualize vessels at risk. In certain patients
and clinical scenarios (intrapelvic implants), close consultation or intraoperative
assistance by a vascular surgeon is necessary.
Intraoperative Risk Mitigation
A thorough understanding of patient anatomy and surgical approach is critical to decrease the
risks of vascular injury.
Surgeons should carefully place retractors, limit limb immobilization, and avoid tourniquet use
in patients at risk.
In certain patients, surgical approaches with vascular assistance may be helpful.

Intraoperative Risk Mitigation
Prevention of vascular injury requires diligence by the surgeon. Placement of retractors
around the acetabulum and the posterior aspect of the knee should be performed
carefully and as safely as possible, using knowledge of specific anatomy to distance
retractors from vessels if possible. The surgeon should avoid positions that create
tension on vessels based on a specific approach during the placement of retractors or
surgical dissection. For example, with the knee in extension, the popliteal vessels may
tent into the surgical field; therefore, any posterior dissection should be performed with
the knee in flexion. Having the hip in extension during the placement of anterior
acetabular retractors may place the vessels at greater risk for injury. The surgeon should
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
15/19

understand the acetabular safe zones during drilling for and placing screws. Tourniquets
should be avoided in patients at risk for thromboembolic occlusion during knee surgery.
In certain patients, a surgical approach may be selected or combined specifically to avoid
vascular injury. In some patients with severe protrusion and implants tenting the pelvic
vessels, a retroperitoneal approach with the vascular team may be necessary to safely
remove implants before reconstruction.
Management
Hemodynamic instability and pulsatile bleeding in the surgical field are causes of immediate
intervention.
Emergent involvement of the vascular surgery team is warranted to recognize direct injury.
A thorough postoperative examination should be undertaken in all patient.
Absent or diminished distal pulses or a cold extremity may represent arterial injury.
Rapid swelling may represent venous injury or occlusion or hematoma formation.
Early imaging studies and vascular consultation are warranted if injury is suspected.
Late diagnosis of pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistulas may be a challenge and requires a
high index of suspicion.

Management
Hemodynamic instability and pulsatile bleeding in the surgical field warrant immediate
attention. If hemodynamic instability occurs, blood and fluid resuscitation should occur
while the cause is explored. If concern for vascular injury exists, even if the injury cannot
be visualized directly (such as with acetabular screw placement), then the vascular
surgery team should be involved immediately. If pulsatile bleeding is encountered and
the vessel is identified in the surgical field, then it should be ligated if possible. If a clear
vascular injury with pulsatile bleeding is identified during knee surgery, a tourniquet
should be inflated while the vascular team is en route. If intra-abdominal vascular injury
suspected during hip surgery, then the hip incision should be stuffed with sterile gauze
and rapidly closed in preparation for emergent laparotomy. The key to patient survival
and mitigation of complications is rapid involvement of the vascular team. Early
identification of a vascular injury will enhance outcomes. Pulses must be assessed at the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Neurovascular Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001026
16/19

end of any hip or knee arthroplasty procedure. For thromboembolic occlusions
diagnosed postoperatively, urgent management is critical for long-term function and to
avoid severe complications, such as amputation. Thrombectomy may not be adequate
because it is associated with a high failure rate, and bypass frequently is necessary.
Surgeons should be aware of ischemic complications, including compartment syndrome,
to appropriately treat the patient during this period, and fasciotomies may be necessary.
If pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistulas are identified in the months or years
postoperatively, prompt vascular referral is warranted, and surgical management usually
is necessary.
Outcomes
Although rare, vascular injuries may be devastating.
The overall mortality rate from a direct vascular injury may be as high as 7%, and a substantial
rate of major amputation has been reported.
Survival and limb salvage is achieved most frequently if high-risk patients are identified
preoperatively and vascular surgery is involved immediately on injury identification.

Outcomes
Vascular injuries may be life- and limb-threatening complications. Direct injury is
associated with a relatively high rate of mortality and major limb amputation. If high-risk
patients are identified preoperatively, risks can be decreased. Early involvement of
vascular surgery results in improved outcomes.
